title: Egypt and the Nile
hookLine: Amr ibn al-As enters Egypt in 640, and over centuries Egypt becomes mostly Muslim

cards: Remember the envoys from Mecca who sailed to Abyssinia with gifts for the Negus, hoping he'd hand the refugees back? Ibn Ishaq names one of them: Amr ibn al-As. He went home empty-handed.
Later he became a Muslim himself, and a commander.
And one day, under the caliph Umar, he leads an army west out of Palestine, across the edge of the desert, toward a green river valley that had been home to kings, temples and churches long before.

teach.h: MISR — THE LAND THAT TOOK YUSUF IN.
teach.b: Egypt in Arabic is Misr, the name the Qur'an uses in the story of Yusuf, where Egypt is the land that takes him in, and where, in the end, his whole family comes to live.

When Amr's army arrived, Egypt was ruled from Constantinople, and in its towns and villages the Arab soldiers met Coptic Christians. Amr took the fortress beside the Nile, and later Alexandria by the sea.
Then he founded a new town on the river bank, Fustat, and built a mosque there. Rebuilt again and again, it still carries his name.

teach.h: TREAT ITS PEOPLE WELL: PROTECTION AND KINSHIP.
teach.b: Before any of this, a hadith in Sahih Muslim says, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions they would one day enter Egypt, and asked them to treat its people well, because they had a claim of protection and of kinship.

Scholars explain the kinship through Hajar, the mother of Ismail, and through Mariyah the Copt, the mother of the Prophet's son Ibrahim. Now the part that's easy to get wrong. Egypt did not become Muslim when Amr arrived.
Historians describe a slow change. Over generations, more and more Egyptians became Muslim, through marriage, through trade, through the pull of the cities, through taxes and law, through faith.
Arabic slowly became the language of the street. And Coptic Christians stayed.
They are still there, in their churches, and the old Coptic language is still sung in their liturgy.
A country's faith didn't change in a battle. It changed in kitchens and markets, one family at a time, across lifetimes.

how: Muslims in Egypt pray in mosques old and new, including the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in Cairo, and live alongside Coptic Christian neighbors whose churches go back to before Islam.

practice: Picture the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in old Cairo: a broad open courtyard under the sky, rows of columns holding up the roof, the noise of the city outside its walls.

Rebuilt again and again and still in use, it has been prayed in by generations who each added a little. If you pray, make a dua for the people who pray there now; if not, simply hold the place in mind.
